摘要

政府出手勒令停售，奇瑞被動展開召回

作者指出，馬來西亞奇瑞針對 Omoda 5 斷軸事件的處理態度相當被動。該事件發生於10月6日，奇瑞卻直到10月11日晚間才發表官方聲明。事實上，馬來西亞陸路交通局（JPJ）早在當天下午就宣布暫時撤銷該車型的型式認證並暫停新車註冊，等同於變相禁售。直到政府介入並要求奇瑞全面審查生產線與供應商後，奇瑞才聲明將啟動召回。作者認為奇瑞並非主動負起責任，而是迫於官方禁令才採取行動，公關應對表現極為差勁。

極端測試的文字遊戲與公關輿論操作

作者進一步以懂車帝測試仰望 U8 煞車踏板斷裂事件為例，說明部分車廠在面對安全質疑時的公關手法。仰望汽車聲稱煞車踏板在「非標準極端工況」下斷裂，僅提供免費升級選項而非正式召回，試圖淡化問題。作者諷刺這種解釋彷彿要求車主在緊急時只能慢速踩煞車。更耐人尋味的是，相關實測影片隨後在多個中國主流社群平台遭到下架或封禁，展現出截然不同的危機處理與輿論控制方式。

奇瑞 OMODA 5 後懸吊脫落奇觀與歷史重演

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解 Karina 與 Converse 聯名廣告如何引發種族歧視爭議，以及爭議雙方各自的解讀。
  • 看見作者如何以完整廣告企劃、圖片裁切與後製方式，質疑單張畫面是否足以證明品牌的意圖。
  • 探討品牌道歉、公眾輿論與社群媒體流量之間的拉扯，以及過度解讀可能帶來的影響。

摘要

廣告畫面引發的爭議

作者以近期廣告爭議為背景，談到 aespa 成員 Karina 與 Converse 合作的「Stars Align with Karina」企劃。廣告中，Karina 穿著白色洋裝、手持黑色鞋款，衣服上的三角形光影原本意在呼應 Converse 的星形標誌；然而，批評者認為三角形讓人聯想到三Ｋ黨的尖頂頭套，而垂在空中的鞋子則讓人聯想到私刑受害者。作者也提到，Converse 馬來西亞帳號曾發布鞋子掛在樹上的圖片，因而遭到類似批評。

作者對「過度解讀」的質疑

作者認為，將廣告畫面解讀成種族主義的人，可能忽略了整體企劃的風格與脈絡。他指出，同一系列其他影像採用高反差、戲劇化、單色商品搭配與 K-pop 偶像時尚元素，並沒有明確的私刑道具、頭套、相關符號或暗示種族歧視的旁白。作者還主張，惹出爭議的畫面是從原本較完整的照片裁切、放大而來，並經過亮度調整；他以翻轉、旋轉、放大佛像再改成紅色的例子，說明透過選擇性編輯，也能把普通圖像塑造成令人不安的聯想。

道歉、政治與社群輿論

作者區分了審查不周與蓄意種族歧視，認為兩者不應被直接畫上等號。他質疑，一家面向全球市場、倚賴年輕消費者的品牌，是否會故意把美國最敏感的種族暴力象徵放進主打廣告；並認為大型企業容易成為道德批判的目標，政治人物與媒體也可能藉此獲得關注。他提到 Converse 撤下廣告、道歉並暫停行銷，也將這類輿論動員與過往「辱華」爭議相比，指出品牌常在輿論壓力下刪除內容、道歉，卻仍可能持續遭到追究。

其他品牌案例與作者的結論

作者接著提及 Dove 廣告中黑人女性換成白人女性的畫面，以及 H&M 印有「叢林裡最酷的猴子」字樣的兒童服裝，作為品牌廣告引發種族爭議的其他例子。他認為 Converse 道歉未必代表品牌真心承認指控，而可能只是降低風險、盡快平息事件；但道歉也未必能終止追問。作者表示，為沒有犯下的錯誤道歉未必是負責任，也可能顯得缺乏立場。最後，他警告，若社會不斷把個人聯想直接等同於企業意圖，未來任何廣告都可能被預先判定有罪；他並指出，Karina 只是拍攝一張手持鞋子的宣傳照，卻因此遭到指控，作者質疑這樣的輿論審判是否還留有公正與法治的空間，並提醒讀者：感到被冒犯，不代表自己必然正確。

================================================

Ads have been running into trouble. lately. Just two episodes ago, I talked. about how Sydney Sweeney sparked. feminist outrage by appearing nude in a. Marc Jacobs ad. Not long after, an. advertisement for the sneaker brand. Converse ran into trouble as well. Everyone, take a look at this photo—. what do you think it looks like? This. ad is for the "Stars Align with Karina" collection, a collaboration between. Karina from the K-pop group aespa and. Converse. The visuals of the ad are. quite simple: Karina is wearing a white. dress, holding a pair of black Converse. sneakers in her left hand. The lighting. casts a triangular shadow on her dress. This was meant to echo the Converse. five-pointed star logo; well, it. certainly echoed something, but it. ended up echoing something else. entirely. Critics argue that this. composition is clearly engaging in. racism. According to them, the pointed. triangle on Karina's white dress looks. like the iconic white pointed hoods of. the KKK. Then there is the image of. Karina holding the shoes in her left. hand, with the shoes dangling in. mid-air. Critics believe that looks. like the feet of a lynching victim. being dangled. I have to say, their. ability to make these associations is. really something. Furthermore, the. Converse Malaysia Instagram account was. caught posting an image of shoes. hanging in a tree, with someone.

climbing a ladder to retrieve them. This was also pointed to as a scene. depicting a lynching. I didn't expect. Malaysia to be involved in this, but. these are two separate matters, so I. won't dwell on that. Some think this is. an over-interpretation, and I count. myself among them. But others do not. think so. Mainstream opinion, civil. rights lawyers, and some U.S. congressmen argue that this ad went. through filming, post-production, and. layers of review. It shouldn't be. brushed off with the excuse that "we. didn't notice." For example,. Representative Troy Carter blasted the. ad, saying Black suffering isn't a. marketing tool, lynching isn't a. creative concept, and the KKK isn't an. aesthetic—the problem is, nobody said. it was. Naturally, he is a Democratic. Representative. Of course the KKK is. not an aesthetic. But the origins of. the KKK are tied to the Democratic. Party. Over a hundred years of. development, the Democratic Party seems. to have turned over a new leaf, but. racism is still hidden in the DNA of. some Democrats. For example, it was. said that if you can't figure out. whether to support me or Trump, then. you aren't Black. New York Governor. Hochul once said that some young Black. kids in the Bronx don't even know what. the word "computer" means, and while. promoting her new book, a governor told. a Black mayor, "I'm just like you, no.

better than you, I got a 960 on my SATs. , I can't read the script." It would. have been fine to just admit you had. bad grades; why add the line "I'm just. like you"? There are plenty of. deep-seated racists within the. Democratic Party, but is this CVERSE ad. actually engaging in racial. discrimination? You have to look at the. entire context of the advertisement to. understand the situation. Within that. same campaign, there are other videos,. stylings, and compositions. Once you. lay out all the other photos from the. dynamic ad, you see it follows a. consistent route of high contrast,. theatricality, stardom, monochrome. product juxtaposition, and K-pop idol. fashion. Looking at the entire campaign. , there are no lynching props, no hoods. , no symbols, and not a single line of. narration that implies racial. discrimination. As long as people are. moving, no one would ever associate. this ad with the KKK, but once you. freeze, zoom, crop, add inflammatory. text and photo editing, it turns into. something sinister. It is said that the. original promotional photo was like. this: Ina in a full-body shot, holding. shoes in her left hand, looking. perfectly normal. The one that sparked. controversy is this zoomed-in, cropped. version of the same photo. That's not. even the worst part; the brightness was. deliberately adjusted, making Ina's. left hand look almost completely black.

If this isn't over-interpretation, then. what is? Well, let's try this. I will. use an even more exaggerated method to. illustrate what over-interpretation is. This is a picture of Buddha. I'll flip. it, rotate it 45 degrees, zoom in, and. turn it red. Look, a Nazi Buddha. Some. might say that even if it wasn't. intentional, CVERSE's lack of. sensitivity in their review process is. still a problem. That is a completely. different level of issue, because being. careless and being racist are two. entirely different things. Yet people. today equate the former with the latter. , and that is precisely. over-interpretation. A brand that. relies on global retail, the Nike. system, and the youth fashion market—. would they intentionally insert. America's most untouchable racial. terror symbols into their flagship. product ad? That's like playing with. fire. It's a death wish. Our brains are. best at seeing exactly what we want to. see. Searching for familiar evils in. gray areas, hijacking others with. political correctness, and then posting. it on social media to farm engagement. and clicks. These are things most. people love to do, especially with big. corporations like CVERSE; they are the. easiest targets. Scolding an unknown. photographer just doesn't get the same. traffic. But if you criticize a brand. under Nike, especially one endorsed by. global stars, the level of traffic is.

extraordinary. Large corporations have. many concerns and cannot easily strike. back at criticism, so politicians can. take advantage of it, and the media can. report that the corporation has. admitted its mistake. The larger the. corporation, the better suited it is to. be the public's moral villain. Because. large corporations have money and PR. departments, these are all "original. sins," especially to those on the left. Therefore, condemning large. corporations is a low-risk,. high-visibility performance of public. morality. Facts have indeed proven this. point. Converse immediately pulled the. ad, apologized, conducted an internal. review, and suspended marketing. There. was absolutely no intention to defend. the original creative. The reaction of. Black Americans to this ad reminds me. of various "insulting China" incidents. over the past decade; the essence of. both is quite similar. "Little Pink" nationalists will single out symbols of. "insulting China," elevate them to. matters of national dignity, and. celebrities will start taking sides. In. the end, the brand is forced to delete. the ad and apologize. Yet, they still. cannot avoid being punished by the. Chinese market in the end. For example,. the D&G ad where a Chinese model uses. chopsticks to eat pizza was deemed an. insult to China. GAP's clothing once. featured a map of China that omitted. Taiwan. Hotels, airlines, and airport.

websites listing Hong Kong and Taiwan. as countries are seen as insulting. China. Even when Western media recently. referred to Tibet as Tibet during a. landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border, it. was considered an insult. Even models. with single eyelids and slanted eyes. are interpreted as demonizing Chinese. people—if single eyelids and small. eyes equal insulting China, then you. should demand the Emperor step down. He. is the one who "insults China" the most. fiercely. Actually, Converse is not the. only victim here. The 2017 Dove ad was. originally intended to express. authenticity, diversity, and continuous. transformation. But the scene where a. Black woman takes off her top to reveal. a White woman was interpreted as a. Black person being "washed white," while the scene where a White woman. takes off her top to reveal a Latina. woman was skipped over and ignored. H&M. also once had a Black child wear their. children's clothing. The shirt read " Coolest Monkey in the Jungle." That was. a bit hard to explain away. The. suspicion of racism cannot be washed. away even with Dove. Although Converse. admitted their mistake and didn't want. to defend themselves, did they truly. feel they were wrong? Certainly not. They apologized only because it was. less costly than refusing to admit a. mistake; they just wanted to get past. the matter as quickly as possible. But. simply kneeling and apologizing won't.

earn forgiveness; it will only invite. further scrutiny. Lawmakers and lawyers. are already demanding that the brand. explain who approved the ad, who filmed. it, and whose idea it was; they want. people to come out and face them. >> So, for me, apologizing for a mistake. you didn't commit isn't being. responsible; it's lacking a stance. Personally, I have no interest in. products that lack any such backbone. But it doesn't really matter anyway. I. never liked these shoes to begin with,. and I like Nike even less. So, don't. misunderstand—this show isn't trying. to whitewash anything for them. The. truly dangerous and terrifying part of. this isn't how much sales plummeted,. but that if the world continues to link. personal associations with corporate. intent, then every future advertisement. will be guilty. A full-body photo of a. woman holding shoes shouldn't have to. carry such heavy historical baggage,. but if you insist that this photo is. related to a lynching, you aren't. entirely wrong. The connection, however. , isn't the history of lynching Black. people, but the fact that the public. has carried out a trial by public. opinion against the brand and the woman. . Just look: such a beautiful woman is. being accused of racism simply because. she took a promotional photo while. holding a pair of shoes. Is there any. justice or rule of law left? >> So, please remember one thing. If you.

constantly feel offended, that's your. own problem. It doesn't mean you're in. the right. Know a little bit of. everything, and life will be a bit more. colorful.
